extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction writers and novice writers seeking craft and career advice
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, craft-focused guidance for writing fiction (and short/long form narrative) covering daily habits, mechanics, elements of story, revision process, and submission/business practices. Based on Stephen King's On Writing as summarized for beginner-to-intermediate writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read a lot
rubrics_metrics.description: To be a good writer, you need to read a lot. Reading exposes you to good and bad writing and helps you recognize the difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King reads ~80 books a year and always carries a book. Read for enjoyment (not only to learn). The more you read, the more you learn about what works and what doesn't.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write a lot / daily writing habit
rubrics_metrics.description: Write regularly with a daily quota to build productivity and momentum—King writes ten pages (~2,000 words) per day and suggests beginners aim for 1,000 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define a writing location and daily time, shut the door, remove distractions, and don't resume other activities until you meet your goal. Take no more than one day off per week to keep momentum and avoid self-doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enjoy the hard work (talent + effort)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sign of talent is enjoying the labor of writing; if the hard work feels like pleasure, you can do it long-term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you don't enjoy reading and writing for their own sake, you likely won't become a good writer. Pleasure in the work sustains consistent practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the truth
rubrics_metrics.description: You can write about anything, but the only requirement is that you tell the truth—truthful writing pulls readers in and makes characters believable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth creates recognizable character behavior and lets readers identify with the story; implausible or unrecognizable characters often break reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master writing mechanics (diction, grammar, phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer is an artisan with tools—diction, grammar, and phrasing—that should be learned and used reliably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult dependable style guides like The Elements of Style (Strunk and White). These mechanics are part of the writer's toolbox and help produce professional, clear prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid passive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Passive constructions make sentences weak; prefer active voice where the subject performs the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of weak passive: 'The car was started by the driver.' 'The discovery was announced with great fanfare.' Convert to active: 'The driver started the car.' Passive voice is described as the refuge of timid, uncertain writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid adverbs (especially -ly modifiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverbs often signal weak writing and blunt the power of verbs; instead make context clear so adverbs become unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: 'Tom started the car dejectedly.' Better: provide context earlier ('Tom sat for ten minutes... He sighed and started the car.'). Delete adverbs that compensate for unclear or weak verbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narration should move the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration is the element that tells what happens and moves the story forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep narration focused on advancing events rather than excessive ornamentation that stalls the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description: provide sensory texture but balance it
rubrics_metrics.description: Description adds sensory detail that draws the reader in, but you must strike a balance—neither too little nor too much description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too little leaves readers without a mental world; too much buries the story. Describe primarily environment and characters to enliven the story without losing the narrative drive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue should sound truthful
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue defines character and should feel real; believable speech makes characters credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid wooden, forced dialogue that grates on the ear. Let characters' speech reflect their personalities and circumstances in a way readers accept as natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't over-plan the plot (avoid rigid plotting)
rubrics_metrics.description: King dislikes pre-planning a story's plot; letting the story emerge naturally reflects the plotlessness of life and keeps the work surprising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over-planning feels artificial and can remove spontaneity and discovery from writing; allow discovery while drafting instead of locking into an elaborate pre-planned plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use literary devices as needed, but sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Tools like symbolism, theme, and backstory are spices—use any tool that enhances the story but don't overdo it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid showing off technique (e.g., excessive alliteration). The point is to tell the story; literary devices should serve the story rather than call attention to themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: First draft: write alone and quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete the first draft without external input; write as quickly as comfortably possible to maintain enthusiasm and limit self-doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't solicit feedback during the first draft because well-meaning comments can create self-doubt or complacency. Finish the draft to preserve momentum and your original energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take a substantial break before revising
rubrics_metrics.description: After finishing the first draft, take time away (King suggests at least six weeks) to gain distance before revising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distance helps you 'kill your darlings' and return with fresh perspective. During the break, write something different rather than tinkering with the draft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision: read in one sitting and address big-picture then specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: When ready to revise, read the draft in one sitting if possible, note fixes, and address both big-picture questions (theme, coherence, recurring elements) and specific issues (grammar, adverbs, plot holes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First make decisions about what the story is about and whether it's coherent; then fix small issues and polish. King recommends doing a second draft after this process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get feedback selectively and incorporate as you like
rubrics_metrics.description: After revising, give the draft to a small group of trusted readers and consider their feedback in your revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a small, trustworthy group. Listen and incorporate advice selectively rather than following all suggestions uncritically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision cycles: King's standard is two drafts plus a polish
rubrics_metrics.description: King's typical process involves writing a first draft, revising in at least a second draft, and then a final polish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use however many revision cycles you need, but King's norm is two substantive drafts and a final polish to finish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build publishing credentials and study markets
rubrics_metrics.description: To build a writing career, get published where you can and study the publications you want to target to learn what they like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with college journals or small magazines, read magazines to understand editorial preferences, and use resources like Writer's Market to find outlets. Build a publishing record before seeking bigger opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish submissions and present professionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Polish your submission materials to look professional: include a brief but meaningful cover letter, print double-spaced on good paper, and show word count clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional presentation increases the chance of being taken seriously by editors and agents. Tailor submissions to each market's expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider getting an agent for larger works
rubrics_metrics.description: As your publishing record grows, consider an agent—particularly if you aim to publish a larger work like a novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents take writers more seriously if they present a professional letter and have a publishing record; an agent can help place larger projects with major publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshops and classes are not shortcuts
rubrics_metrics.description: Attending workshops, classes, or seminars is not a guaranteed path to success; there are no shortcuts to becoming a writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best way to learn is still to read a lot and write a lot; important lessons are often learned independently through practice rather than relying on programs.
